item.title: Benchmarking and Experimental Validation of Machine Learning Strategies for Enzyme Engineering
item.description:
Abstract
Enzyme-directed evolution increasingly relies on computational tools to prioritize mutations, yet their practical value is difficult to assess because kinetic data are often aggregated across heterogeneous assay conditions, inflating apparent generalization. Here we introduce EnzyArena, a curated benchmark in which kinetic parameters (kcat, Km, or kcat/Km) are grouped by experimental campaign and measured under matched conditions, thereby minimizing confounders such as pH, temperature, reaction, and batch. Using EnzyArena, we systematically evaluate 20 models spanning four widely used strategies for guiding enzyme evolution: protein–ligand binding affinity prediction, protein stability prediction, zero-shot fitness prediction and enzyme kinetic parameters prediction. Across subsets derived from public databases and 25 literature-derived mutagenesis data sets, most models exhibit weak, fragile, or inconsistent correlation with measured functional outcomes. Kinetic-parameter predictors perform strongly on database-derived subsets but lose their advantage on literature-derived mutagenesis data sets, whereas zero-shot predictors show more consistent generalization. A simple consensus of multiple zero-shot models further improves the precision of identifying beneficial mutants in retrospective analyses. We prospectively validated these findings in a wet-lab campaign (150 mutants) comparing random mutants, UniKP-prioritized mutants, and ESM-1v-prioritized mutants (representing supervised kinetic parameters prediction and zero-shot fitness prediction, respectively), where ESM-1v achieved the highest utility and UniKP underperformed the random baseline. Together, this study establishes realistic baselines for computational mutant prioritization and indicates that zero-shot strategies provide the most consistent, although still modest, performance among the approaches evaluated.

item.title: Modeling the Soil Dissipation Kinetics of Small Molecules
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding the metabolic fate of small molecules is central to risk assessment and the rational design of plant protection products, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and food additives. In environmental systems, dissipation is governed by kinetic processes operating across soil, water, and other compartments. For chemicals released into the environment, especially active ingredients of plant protection products, assessing soil persistence is an essential regulatory requirement. The ability to predict soil persistence, ideally in advance of commissioning experiments, is highly valuable for identifying novel active ingredients for plant protection products. Here, we introduce machine learning models that predict the full time course of small-molecule dissipation in soil. These models are explicitly constrained by mechanistic assumptions encoded as ordinary differential equations (ODEs). By design, this physics-constrained parametrization enforces physical plausibility. To the best of our knowledge, our models are the first to predict soil dissipation kinetics from molecular structures using a constrained time course framework. We found that this framework almost always outperformed a conventional QSAR approach of predicting prefitted kinetic parameters. We further investigated the incorporation of soil metadata, i.e., predefined and experimentally measured soil parameters, into the model, with mixed results. Our framework supports screening and design decisions by linking molecular properties and soil metadata to predicted environmental lifetimes and dissipation profiles.

item.title: QRxVision: Multimodal QR Encoding and Computer Vision for Domain-Specific Drug Discovery
item.description:
Abstract
Computational approaches applied to the drug discovery pipeline are invaluable because of their overall speed or time to solution, sustainability, accessibility combined with ever improving accuracy. Furthermore, the high-throughput virtual screening supports practical sampling of the vast chemical space for target-relevant bioactive compounds that can be experimentally validated further downstream in the drug development process. The current paradigm being practiced in computer-aided drug screening strategies centers around structure-based and ligand-based approaches supported by a range of computational tools including de novo design, molecular dynamics-based approaches, and machine learning (ML). Overall, the latter approach has shown great promise generating models of high computational speed coupled with good accuracy. In this work, we developed QRxVision, a domain-specific multimodal ML model explicitly optimized for kinase target assignment using similarity-based profile matching and retrieval. QRxVision utilizes image vision from a pretrained VGG16 (Visual Geometry Group–16) model for deep spatial feature extraction and cosine similarity calculation. By encoding drug multimodality-associated parameters (MAP) into standardized QR code images, QRxVision can evaluate the similarity between test and reference compounds. Drug targets can then be assigned via transitive profile matching. Validation using kinase inhibitors shows that QRxVision is 71% successful at assigning viable small molecules within the Top-5 predictions (p-value < 0.05). Overall, we believe that with the appropriate algorithmic modifications and domain retargeting, the QRxVision framework can be applied to other target assignment tasks.

item.title: C-MAGE: Automated Extraction and Organization Engine for Molecular Representations in Chemical Documents
item.description:
Abstract
To exploit the data present in chemical literature for AI applications in chemistry, an expanded and reliable extraction pipeline is needed. AI-ready chemical databases broaden chemical space coverage and provide benchmarking and training sets for machine learning model development to drive innovation within the field. To curate data from chemical documents, a multimodal approach is needed. C-MAGE is an open-source molecule extraction engine that processes figures and tables in PDF files to provide machine-readable molecule data sets of the structures as CXSMILES strings, an encompassing representation that evades heuristic translation of superatoms to SMILES subunits. This led to a 7.1% increase in accurate molecular representations generated. All data extracted undergo confidence-based sorting to ensure high precision (77.6%) in data set collection and remove the need for manually sorting data point validity. Both the CXSMILES and their confidence values are reproducible and are generated efficiently (1.7 s per molecule). C-MAGE’s use is demonstrated by the generation of an annotated data set containing 1454 CXSMILES strings from 38 chemical documents. C-MAGE thus enables large-scale information extraction of chemical structures in a consistent and reproducible pipeline, complementing the more common text extractions.

item.title: Antimicrobial Peptide Databases and Prediction Tools: Toward a Standard Evaluation Framework
item.description:
Abstract
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has a profound impact on animal and human health and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and public health costs. There is a clear need to develop novel, effective antibiotic agents, which can overcome the current AMR crisis. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) may offer such a solution and have attracted growing attention for their potential to combat AMR. In parallel, the growing availability of peptide sequences in public databases has stimulated the development of numerous machine learning and deep learning tools to predict antimicrobial activity computationally. However, it remains unclear how reliably these tools can be compared, as existing studies often rely on heterogeneous data sets and inconsistent evaluation protocols that may lead to data leakage and inflated performance estimates. This raises a central question: what evaluation criteria and benchmark resources are needed to enable fair, reproducible, and biologically meaningful assessment of AMP prediction tools? We address this question by focusing specifically on antibacterial peptides (ABPs). We first provide an overview of AMP databases relevant to antibacterial activity and compare their content, redundancy, and experimental metadata. We then critically assess existing computational tools for ABP prediction, highlighting key limitations related to data set construction, affinity to certain sequences, data leakage, and inconsistent performance reporting. Based on these limitations, we propose a reference evaluation framework designed to improve comparability, reproducibility, and practical utility in ABP prediction. Finally, we provide targeted recommendations for AMP databases and future tool development to support more robust progress in the computational discovery of ABPs.

item.title: LESS-PseU: A Language Model-Enhanced Semistacking Framework for RNA Pseudouridine Site Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate prediction of RNA pseudouridine (Ψ) sites remains challenging because existing models often struggle to integrate interpretable handcrafted features with high-dimensional contextual representations from pretrained genomic language models. To address this issue, we propose LESS-PseU, a language model-enhanced semistacking framework that fuses the predicted probability features of primary learners with DNABERT2 embeddings for multiple species Ψ site prediction. Specifically, we first built three primary learners based on three kinds of hand-crafted features, including one-hot, k-mer, and nucleotide chemical property features. Instead of training a primary learner based on the embeddings extracted from DNABERT2, the embeddings were directly concatenated with the predicted probabilities of the three primary learners as the input features for a Logistic Regression meta-learner for final prediction. Under a leakage-aware cross-validation setting, our model was validated on the training sets of three species. Furthermore, on independent test sets from human, mouse, and yeast, LESS-PseU achieved AUC values of 0.9069, 0.8833, and 0.8820, respectively, which were higher than those of the compared models. A Friedman test indicated an overall difference (p = 0.029). Paired DeLong tests further showed that the AUC improvements over Meta-PseU were significant for the human and mouse data sets, while those over PseU-ST were significant for all three species. Ablation analysis, fusion-strategy comparison, and pretrained language-model comparison further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Additional evaluations on m5C and m7G benchmarks provided preliminary evidence that the framework may be applicable to other RNA modification prediction tasks.

item.title: Sustainable Design of Deep Eutectic Solvent Viscosity: A Structure–Property Machine Learning Framework with Structure-Disjoint Validation
item.description:
Abstract
Deep eutectic solvents (DES) have emerged as sustainable alternatives to conventional organic solvents, yet their industrial adoption remains hindered by limited predictive capability for transport properties, particularly viscosity. This work reports a machine learning framework for DES viscosity prediction built on 3440 experimental measurements spanning 237 systems (85 hydrogen bond acceptors, 86 hydrogen bond donors), with viscosities from 1.3 to 85,000 mPa·s over 278–378 K, in which component identity is defined by canonical isomeric SMILES rather than by name and structural assignments have been audited and corrected. A hierarchical feature engineering strategy generated 236 candidate descriptors, reduced to 128 modeling features by removing noncomputable, monotonically redundant and collinear terms, with no imputation of missing values at any stage. Ten algorithms spanning linear, kernel, neural and tree-ensemble families were benchmarked under identical tuning and evaluation; support vector regression achieved the lowest cross-validated error (R2 = 0.974, AARD = 12.2%) against 42% for linear models, establishing that nonlinearity accounts for two-thirds of the achievable error reduction. The central result is a quantified separation between interpolation and extrapolation obtained on identical data and a single model: AARD is 13% on a random hold-out, 75% for an unseen acceptor under structure-disjoint leave-one-HBA-out validation, 129% for an unseen donor, and 145% for an unseen chemical family. This 10-fold spread demonstrates that a single reported accuracy figure is uninterpretable for DES property models unless the splitting protocol is stated. Global SHAP attribution on the final model assigns 31.4% of total contribution to composition-weighted mixing descriptors and 23.7% to asymmetry descriptors quantifying HBA–HBD dissimilarity, establishing both families as substantial and nonredundant. The framework integrates gradient-free inverse design on a smooth surrogate, application-oriented clustering by viscosity and Arrhenius activation energy, and manufacturing robustness assessment, providing actionable tools for rational DES formulation together with explicit and empirically measured boundaries on their use.

item.title: Geometry-Aware Molecular Representation Learning for Approximating NORMAN-Predicted Retention Time Indices in Nontargeted Screening
item.description:
Abstract
Retention information provides chromatographic evidence complementary to mass spectrometric data in LC-HRMS nontargeted screening (NTS), yet many existing models rely mainly on 1D SMILES or 2D molecular graphs and make limited use of three-dimensional structure. Here, we developed ViSRTI (Vector-Interaction-Spatial Retention Time Index), a ViSNet-based geometry-aware framework that integrates 3D molecular representations with multimodal descriptors to model the precomputed positive- and negative-mode RTI labels in NORMAN SusDat. On fixed held-out test sets, ViSRTI-G outperformed all three baselines. Relative to the best-performing baseline for each metric, R2 increased by 0.022 (vs GNN-RT) and 0.025 (vs SMILES-BiLSTM), while MAE decreased by 5.39 and 6.56 RTI units (both vs SMILES-BiLSTM) in positive and negative modes, respectively. Incremental feature integration and SHAP-guided retraining identified ViSRTI-GP with KOC and LogP masked for positive mode and ViSRTI-GPT for negative mode, achieving R2 values of 0.9433 and 0.9258 and MAEs of 40.42 and 40.76 RTI units, respectively. Under Bemis–Murcko scaffold-disjoint 5-fold cross-validation, R2 remained at 0.9114 ± 0.0126 and 0.8937 ± 0.0117, indicating substantial agreement for unseen scaffold groups. Laboratory-specific RT-RTI calibration using 21 standards yielded R2 values of 0.8575 and 0.9525 in positive and negative modes. In a benzo[a]pyrene/benzo[e]pyrene case study, calibration-derived expected RTs differed from measured values by only 0.28 and 0.11 min, respectively, and reproduced the observed elution order. Overall, ViSRTI provides a geometry-aware surrogate for NORMAN-predicted RTI and enables laboratory-specific conversion of predicted RTI into complementary retention-time constraints for candidate evaluation in NTS.

item.title: Modulating Transthyretin Fibril Stability with D-Retro-Inverso Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
A major cause of heart failure in elderly patients is the deposition of transthyretin (TTR) fibrils. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we explore how the stability of TTR fibrils can be modulated by D-retro-inverso (DRI) peptides, built from D-amino acids with the sequence of the parent peptide switched. We screened a library of peptide candidates generated from aggregation-prone regions in the TTR sequence, including peptides from WALTZ-DB 2.0 database of amyloid peptides, and selected three peptides based on their potential to disrupt interactions in a structurally flexible region of the fibril. Peptides were docked to the surface of the TTR fibril using HADDOCK 2.4, followed by all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate peptide–fibril interactions and their effects on fibril structure. We finally describe a potential mechanism by which one of these peptides, DRI-K6V, perturbs the structural integrity of TTR fibrils, and identify the segment K80-S100 as a potential target for modulating TTR fibril stability. Our results may open the way to the design of peptide drugs targeting established TTR amyloidosis.

item.title: DBNAMP: A Chemically Curated Database of Noncanonical Antimicrobial Peptides with Standardized Molecular Representations
item.description:
Abstract
Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising anti-infective agents, yet conventional sequence-centered resources often inadequately represent noncanonical residues, stereochemical variations, terminal modifications, cyclization, lipidation, stapling, and peptidomimetic scaffolds, limiting chemically meaningful annotation, comparison, and structure–activity relationship analysis. Here, we present DBNAMP, a manually curated and chemically explicit database of AMP-like entities containing residue-level noncanonical features, molecular-level covalent modifications, or both; it currently comprises 1,859 curated entries, including 1,421 entries with computed representative three-dimensional conformers and 129 standardized controlled-vocabulary records for noncanonical residues and peptide modifications. Among 537 source-level ambiguity-audit records, 84 remained unresolved after review, of which 82 retained at least one uppercase X character. Only one such record was included in the final release. Each DBNAMP entry integrates sequence, chemical annotation, antimicrobial activity, target organisms, physicochemical descriptors, molecular representations, structural information, and literature or patent provenance. In addition to browsing, filtering, and data download, DBNAMP enables chemically informed exploration of related peptide entities through standardized molecular representations and incorporates a lightweight SMILES-based prioritization module for preliminary ranking of candidate molecules. By bridging sequence-level peptide annotation and chemically explicit molecular representation, DBNAMP supports chemoinformatics analysis, structure–activity relationship studies, virtual screening, and computer-aided design of chemically diverse AMP candidates and is freely accessible at https://dbnamp.cn/.

item.title: Design Trade-Offs between Target Binding and Self-Association Revealed by De Novo SARS-CoV-2 Binders
item.description:
Abstract
De novo protein binders have emerged as a powerful platform for molecular recognition, yet achieving high affinity while maintaining favorable biophysical properties remains a major challenge. Here, using the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) as a model target, we generated two de novo protein binder design campaigns that deliberately imposed different trade-offs between binding and monomeric behavior, and benchmarked them against a set of experimentally validated binders. Through integrated experimental and computational analyses, we show that binder design is constrained by two distinct failure modes that require different optimization strategies. None of the 22 original designs showed measurable binding to the RBD, with one class remaining monomeric but failing to achieve sufficient target binding, while the other had more competent binding interfaces but exhibited excessive surface hydrophobicity that promoted self-association. By integrating AlphaFold-based predictions, molecular dynamics simulations, docking analyses, and surface aggregation propensity (SAP) calculations, we establish complementary computational signatures that distinguish these failure modes and reveal their underlying structural determinants. Guided by these insights, we prospectively redesigned a representative failed binder by reducing noninterface hydrophobicity while preserving folding and binding interface quality. Experimental characterization by SEC-MALS, surface plasmon resonance, and circular dichroism confirmed that the redesigned variants were stable monomers and acquired low μM binding affinities. Together, our results define the mechanistic trade-offs between binding and self-association in de novo protein binder design and provide a framework for diagnosing and rationally overcoming common design failure modes.

item.title: Pharmacophore-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Ligand-Based De Novo Drug Design
item.description:
Abstract
Developing bioactive molecules remains a central, time- and cost-heavy challenge in drug discovery, particularly for novel targets lacking structural or functional data. Pharmacophore modeling presents an alternative for capturing the key features required for molecular bioactivity against a biological target. In this work, we present PharmaDiff, a pharmacophore-conditioned diffusion model for 3D molecular generation. PharmaDiff employs a transformer-based architecture to integrate an atom-based representation of the 3D pharmacophore into the generative process, enabling the precise generation of 3D molecular graphs that align with predefined pharmacophore hypotheses. Through comprehensive testing, PharmaDiff demonstrates superior performance in matching 3D pharmacophore constraints compared to ligand-based drug design methods. Additionally, it achieves higher docking scores across a range of proteins in structure-based drug design, without the need for target protein structures. By integrating pharmacophore modeling with 3D generative techniques, PharmaDiff offers a powerful and flexible framework for rational drug design.

item.title: Evaluating Drug–Drug Interactions by Constructing Advanced Machine Learning Models of ABC Transporter Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters play a critical role in transmembrane transport, and the inhibition of ABC transporter-mediated efflux can lead to unintended drug–drug interactions (DDIs). The identification of new drug candidates as perpetrators of transporter-mediated DDIs requires synthesis of significant drug products and costly experimental evaluation. Alternatively, computational approaches can rapidly and accurately screen the DDI liability of new drug candidates in silico. Here, we developed a novel DDI risk assessment protocol incorporating classic and graph-based quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models. These models were trained on publicly available, large-scale, structurally diverse in vitro chemical inhibition data for P-gp, BCRP, and MRP1. The resultant models yielded promising R2 scores (0.58 to 0.82). External predictions successfully identified inhibitors, verified by experimental validation or literature review, and detected drugs with the potential to perpetrate clinically relevant DDIs. In summary, we developed a large, diverse database of ABC transporter inhibitors and present an applicable alternative protocol that incorporates model predictions to evaluate transporter-mediated DDIs for new drug candidates to prevent potentially harmful clinical outcomes.

item.title: Small-Molecule 1 H and 13 C NMR: From Chemical-Shift Prediction to Automated Structure Elucidation
item.description:
Abstract
1H and 13C NMR chemical-shift prediction has progressed from empirical rules and experimental databases to graph neural networks, three-dimensional molecular representations, and approaches that integrate quantum chemistry with machine learning; its applications have likewise expanded from chemical-shift calculation for known structures to experimental spectral assignment, candidate-structure discrimination, and automated structure elucidation. Forward structure-to-NMR prediction can generate predicted spectral-library data for candidate molecules and support structure retrieval and candidate screening by matching predicted and experimental chemical shifts; inverse NMR-to-structure analysis progressively constrains the candidate space using structural constraints encoded in experimental spectra. This Review systematically surveys the development and growing integration of these two directions, focusing on how chemical-shift prediction contributes to peak-to-atom assignment, candidate-structure comparison, and automated structure elucidation, and examining how prediction error, candidate coverage, and experimental data quality affect final structural decisions. More recently, agentic approaches have begun to organize existing NMR prediction and structure-elucidation tools into iterative analytical systems that continuously update candidate structures from current spectroscopic evidence and select subsequent computational or experimental operations; further progress in automated structure elucidation depends on reliable predicted spectral libraries, clearly defined model applicability domains, and structural conclusions that can be tested against experimental spectroscopic evidence.

item.title: DockBind: A Quality-Controlled Data Set of Modeled Protein–Ligand Complexes Associated with Affinity Data
item.description:
Abstract
Ligand–protein interaction prediction is essential for structure-based drug discovery, but further development of machine-learning scoring functions is limited by a lack of high-quality training data sets. Here, we present DockBind, a curated data set of modeled protein–ligand complexes paired with experimental binding affinity data, generated through a quality-controlled docking workflow. This workflow was developed based on an expanded docking benchmark, where we systematically evaluated free and template-based docking methods as well as ligand similarity and maximum common substructure (MCS)-based pose filtering to generate and identify the most realistic poses. The resulting workflow was then incorporated into a pipeline integrating structural and binding affinity data from Binding MOAD, the Protein Data Bank, ChEMBL, and BindingDB, which resulted in 18,332 complexes across 612 protein targets, with high structural reliability and chemical diversity─the DockBind data set─providing a valuable resource for training and benchmarking machine-learning scoring functions.

item.title: Insights into Composition-Induced Structural Shifts in Lipid Nanoparticles
item.description:
Abstract
Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading platform for nucleic acid delivery, yet current formulations typically suffer from rapid in vivo clearance and limited extrahepatic delivery. Recent experiments demonstrate that increasing the helper lipid content (e.g., to 40% 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine [DSPC]) can significantly improve mRNA stability, prolong circulation, and enhance transfection efficiency. In this study, we used coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to provide mechanistic insight into the structural changes driving these improvements. Our simulations confirm that an elevated helper lipid content fundamentally alters the internal morphology of the LNP. Consistent with experimental observations, at high DSPC levels, the core transitions from a compact, disordered, predominantly lipid state to an extended structure with distinct lamellar-like elements encompassing lipid-rich and water-rich regions. This structural reorganization can be used to rationalize the enhanced stability and delivery properties reported in the experiments. These findings provide a molecular-level understanding of the composition-morphology relationship and suggest that coarse-grained modeling can inform the design of novel LNP formulations.

item.title: Systematic Profiling of Encoder Architectures and Multimodal Embeddings in Protein Foundation Models Reveals Data Set-Driven Separability Regimes in Prediction of Allosteric and Orthosteric Binding Sites
item.description:
Abstract
Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

item.title: From Random Splits to Unseen Solvents: Quantum-Chemistry-Derived Surface Descriptors Improve Solubility Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Solvent screening often requires predictions for solvents that are absent from the training data. Using 103,262 aligned BigSolDB v2.1 records, we constructed a fixed solvent-level OOD benchmark in which five solvent identities were excluded from model training, validation, early stopping, SHAP ranking, and feature selection. A compact RDKit two-dimensional baseline reaches an IID R2 = 0.954 ± 0.001 under random splitting but falls to an OOD R2 = 0.541 ± 0.019 on the held-out solvents. Under the same benchmark, adding Gasteiger charge proxies and monomer-level GFN2-xTB/COSMO σ-moment surface descriptors raises the OOD R2 to 0.756 ± 0.007. A validation-selected 47-feature representation that also includes deterministic solute–solvent compatibility features reaches an OOD R2 = 0.788 ± 0.008, an MAE = 0.413, and an RMSE = 0.574 log10 S unit under the 20-seed protocol. The improvement depends on solvent identity: DMSO, NMP, and cyclohexane show the largest error reductions, ethylene glycol changes little, and n-propyl acetate is slightly worse than the electrostatic baseline. Learner controls and pair-xTB calculations are used as supporting checks; optimized 1:1 dimers and small 1:2/2:1 clusters do not improve the fixed-OOD result. MICA v0.2 distributes the frozen 20-seed ensemble for prepared-descriptor inference with ensemble-disagreement summaries, applicability-domain flags, and solvent-ranking reports.

item.title: AI-Driven Discovery Pipeline Identifies Carvedilol as a Novel Partial Agonist of THRβ
item.description:
Abstract
Thyroid hormone receptor beta (THRβ) is a key therapeutic target for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and dyslipidemia, yet the discovery of structurally diverse agonists remains challenging. Here, we developed an AI-driven hierarchical drug discovery framework integrating graph neural network (GNN)-based virtual screening, structure-based modeling, and multilevel biological validation to accelerate THRβ agonist identification. The optimized GNN model outperformed conventional machine-learning approaches and enabled efficient prioritization of active compounds from an in-house library. Subsequent molecular docking and MM/GBSA rescoring identified Carvedilol as a high-confidence candidate. TR-FRET assays confirmed that Carvedilol acts as a partial THRβ agonist with preferential SRC2-2 coactivator recruitment, comparable to Resmetirom. Cellular assays further demonstrated that Carvedilol significantly reduced lipid accumulation and triglyceride levels and upregulated key metabolic regulators, including DIO1, ME1, and LDLR. Molecular dynamics and dcTMD analyses elucidated that Carvedilol is stabilized within the ligand-binding pocket through dominant hydrophobic interactions and specific hydrogen bonds with Thr273 and His435. Overall, this study repurposes Carvedilol as a structurally distinct THRβ agonist and validates an effective AI-guided strategy for nuclear receptor-targeted drug discovery.

item.title: HEIWA: Hybrid Explicit–Implicit Water Attention Affects Force Field Accuracy in Structure-Based Protein Language Model ESM3
item.description:
Abstract
Protein language models have achieved remarkable success in structure prediction and de novo design. However, their understanding of physical interactions remains limited. For structure-based models, we hypothesize that this limitation stems from the absence of explicit solvent modeling: water mediates hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic burial, and electrostatic interactions that govern protein thermodynamics and kinetics, yet current structure-based models treat proteins as if they exist in a vacuum. Using thermophilic protein classification as a proxy task for force-field awareness, per-residue logit mis-correlated with H-bonds as a destabilizing attribute and exhibits significant solvent-accessible surface area (SASA)-dependent error, despite high overall classification accuracy. These artifacts point to the water–protein interface as a source of systematic bias. To address this, we propose HEIWA (HybridExplicit-Implicit Water Attention), a novel attention module that injects solvent-mediated force-field information into static ESM3 residue embeddings via an all-query-to-all-key water–residue attention. Biophysics-guided model selection identifies configurations whose residue-level outputs are more consistent with the RMSF benchmark and selected biophysical attributes, while classification performance remains broadly comparable to the baseline. By forcing the model to predict the protein thermophilicity from the contributions of individual residues, HEIWA learns biophysical patterns that can be extended to SUPFAM absent from the training data set. HEIWA also largely preserves the embedding structure of ESM3. Molecular dynamics simulations show improved kinetic stability under thermophilic conditions, suggesting the potential to generate structures with greater kinetic stability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to incorporate explicit solvent encoding into a residue-resolution protein language model.

item.title: Drugging Pockets at the Surface of c-MYC Oncoproteins Revealed by Well-Tempered Metadynamics
item.description:
Abstract
The MYC oncogene encodes a master transcription factor essential for regulating cellular homeostasis, growth, and metabolism. However, its deregulation is involved in up to 70% of human cancers, where it drives uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Structurally, MYC is characterized by an N-terminal transactivation domain and a C-terminal bHLHLZ domain critical for DNA binding and dimerization with MAX. Despite its clinical significance, MYC has remained historically “undruggable” due to its intrinsically disordered structure and the absence of traditional binding pockets. In this study, we combined all-atom Molecular Dynamics and well-tempered metadynamics simulations to map the conformational landscape of a MYC motif in aqueous ionic solution. The selected energy-minimized structures exhibit stable conformations and drugging pockets, providing structural foundations for targetting c-MYC. Furthermore, both the electrostatic potential and docking results for the obtained structure and the MYC inhibitor’s 10074-G5 demonstrated excellent fit, highlighting its potential as a drug target. This inhibitor, introduced in several previously unpublished drugging pockets, maintained a steady binding to MYC over unbiased trajectories lasting 1 μs. These findings provide a previously uncharacterized structural foundation for the design of innovative therapeutic interventions, such as small-molecule inhibitors or peptides aimed at disrupting oncogenic MYC activity.

item.title: AlphaFold3 Pseudo-Ensembles Capture β-Sheet Organization and Structural Diversity of Short Amyloidogenic Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
Beyond predicting unique native globular protein structures, AlphaFold has been used to sample conformational diversity in globular proteins. Here, we asked whether this capacity can be transferred to amyloid fibrils formed by short peptides, despite the fundamental difficulties posed by their polymorphism, sensitivity to environmental variables such as pH and cofactors, limited evolutionary constraints, and underrepresentation of amyloids in structural databases. Using a comprehensive set of short amyloidogenic peptides, we show that sets of AlphaFold3 (AF3) models (pseudo-ensembles) are accurate predictors of parallel versus antiparallel β-sheet organization, correctly assigning 112 of the 117 peptides for which a clear preference is predicted. Moreover, the simultaneous sampling of both organizations provides a signature of structural diversity, as shown for the polymorphic peptides MVGGVVIA and LYIQWL. Modeling of the precise steric-zipper architecture is less reliable and biased toward compact arrangements, while prediction in the presence of cosolvents and metal ions does not reproduce solvent-mediated interfaces or noncanonical coordination geometries. Thus, although AF3 does not fully capture the physicochemical complexity of amyloid assemblies, its pseudo-ensembles provide a rapid and useful approach for predicting β-sheet organization and identifying amyloidogenic sequences with potential structural diversity.

item.title: Efficient and Accurate Ligand Strain Calculations in Solution with the AIMNet2 Neural Network Potential
item.description:
Abstract
Conformational strain, the energy a ligand pays to adopt its bound conformation, contributes to binding affinity but is routinely misestimated. The standard estimate references a single gas-phase energy minimum. This ignores solvent and mishandles charged ligands: in vacuo their intramolecular electrostatics collapse them into compact minima that deflate the unbound reference and inflate the apparent strain. We introduce AIMNet2-CPCM, a neural network potential trained to B97-3c energies and forces in a conductor-like continuum solvent (CPCM). It treats neutral and charged species on the same footing, and its batched GPU inference makes a solvated global-minimum search practical across an entire screening library. Across ∼8K PDB ligands the solvated strain has a median of 4.0 kcal/mol and rises with net charge. The trend is well determined through a net charge of −2. The −3 and −4 polyanions dominate the high-strain tail, where continuum solvation is least reliable, and their values are reported as upper bounds. Gas-phase force fields reproduce the neutral strains but overstate the charged ones, because they collapse the unbound minimum that solvent screening keeps open. Adding a continuum solvent to the force field removes most of this error and confirms the mechanism. Profiling at this scale further shows that the same ligand strains very differently across the targets that bind it: ligand strain is a property of the bound pose, not a transferable molecular descriptor.

item.title: Structure Prototype Learning for Federated Molecular Property Prediction under Scaffold Heterogeneity
item.description:
Abstract
Federated molecular property prediction enables collaboration across private chemical libraries, but parameter averaging does not explicitly account for scaffold heterogeneity. FedSPL groups molecules using fixed descriptors and exchanges embedding prototypes alongside model parameters, enabling label-independent prototype matching while retaining supervised property prediction. Across five classification benchmarks and three heterogeneity levels, matched three-seed evaluation using masked, held-out server-model ROC-AUC showed higher mean final AUC than FedAvg in seven of 15 settings. Consistently positive differences on SIDER and mixed outcomes elsewhere indicate data set-dependent benefits, motivating validation-guided use of structural information in federated prototype learning.

item.title: Benchmarking Protein–Ligand Cofolding Models: Correct Ligand Placement Is Decoupled From Accurate Protein Conformation
item.description:
Abstract
AI-driven cofolding models have become central tools for predicting protein–ligand complexes, yet it remains unclear whether the resulting structures recover the correct protein conformation or merely place the ligand plausibly within an otherwise mispredicted fold. Here, we benchmark four state-of-the-art cofolding models, AlphaFold3, RoseTTAFold3, Boltz-2, and Chai-1, and show that correct ligand placement is systematically decoupled from accurate prediction of the surrounding protein conformation. As test systems, we use kinases and Class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), families whose pharmacology depends on well-defined conformational states. To enable a prospective assessment, we evaluate complexes released after the training cutoffs of all tested models, together with one earlier nucleotide-bound structure as a control. We find that state-defining structural features, including kinase activation-loop, DFG/DYG geometries, and GPCR intracellular conformations such as ICL3, are frequently mispredicted even when ligand root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) is low. Cofolding adaptively remodels the orthosteric pocket around the bound ligand, but this local adaptation rarely propagates to the correct global conformation. Incorporating state-annotated templates and filtered multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) improves conformational recovery in some cases but has little effect in others, and model confidence metrics correlate with small-molecule placement but cannot report whether the local pocket geometry was recovered. Furthermore, while orthosteric ligand placement is generally reliable, the single allosteric complex in our set is misplaced by all models, even under explicit guidance. These results identify conformational decoupling as a fundamental limitation of current cofolding approaches across the systems evaluated, with direct implications for state-selective and structure-based drug design.

item.title: GLH 2 Syn: Global–Local Dual-View Heterogeneous Hypergraph Learning for Drug Synergy Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Drug combination therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for improving therapeutic efficacy. While hypergraphs have demonstrated substantial potential for high-order drug synergy modeling, existing approaches still suffer from two critical limitations: (1) reliance on locally determined aggregation limits the utilization of multihop topological context and broader structural information across the hypergraph; (2) homogeneous message passing overlooks the structural heterogeneity of drugs and cell lines within hyperedges. To address these issues, we propose GLH2Syn, a global–local dual-view heterogeneous hypergraph learning framework for drug synergy prediction. Specifically, GLH2Syn operates on a heterogeneous hypergraph in which each drug–drug–cell line triplet forms a hyperedge, incorporating two complementary views: a global diffusion view and a local topology view. The global diffusion view performs diffusion over the node–hyperedge topology to derive globally informed incidence weights, thereby incorporating structural context into local aggregation. The local topology view captures fine-grained structural heterogeneity within hyperedges through structure-aware node-hyperedge propagation, distinguishing the heterogeneous roles of drugs and cell lines in high-order interactions. Furthermore, we design a joint optimization objective integrating drug synergy prediction with similarity reconstruction to preserve both predictive accuracy and biological consistency. Extensive experiments on two public data sets demonstrate that GLH2Syn consistently outperforms 11 competitive baselines on both classification and regression tasks across three test scenarios. Case studies further validate its potential in discovering novel synergistic drug combinations.

item.title: Reducing Data Requirements for Sequence–Property Prediction in Copolymer Compatibilizers via Deep Neural Network Tuning
item.description:
Abstract
Synthetic sequence-controlled polymers promise to transform polymer science by combining the chemical versatility of synthetic polymers with the precise sequence-mediated functionality of biological proteins. However, design of these materials has proven extraordinarily challenging, because they lack the massive data sets of closely related evolved molecules that accelerate design of proteins. Here, we report on an Artificial Intelligence strategy to reduce the amount of data necessary to accelerate the design of these materials. We focus on data connecting the repeat-unit-sequence of a model compatibilizer molecule to its ability to reduce the interfacial tension between distinct polymer domains. The optimal sequence of these molecules, which are essential for applications such as mixed-waste polymer recycling, depends strongly on variables such as concentration and chemical details of the polymer. We show that a deep neural network trained on low-fidelity data for sequence/interfacial tension relations at one set of conditions can be rapidly tuned to make higher-fidelity predictions at a distinct set of conditions, requiring far less data than would ordinarily be needed within the data sets we have tested. This priming using a pretrained model and then tuning it on unseen data from a different data set approach could allow a single low-fidelity parent data set to accelerate prediction and design in a larger set of related systems.

item.title: A Multimodal Geometric Learning Framework for Interpretable Peptide Toxicity Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Peptide therapeutics are promising drug candidates because of their high activity and specificity. However, their potential toxicity poses a major hurdle, making accurate computational toxicity predictions urgently necessary for early safety screening. Existing methods largely rely on sequence data or simple graph representations, thereby limiting their ability to capture higher-order physicochemical interactions. To address this, we propose MBFGNK, an interpretable multimodal geometric learning framework, for peptide toxicity prediction. It integrates sequence representations from pretrained protein language models, 3D structural features via an equivariant graph neural network (EGNN), and physicochemical hypergraph representations capturing global, local, and biologically synergistic residue interactions. A modality attention gate adaptively fuses these heterogeneous data types, while a Chebyshev polynomial-based Kolmogorov–Arnold network (ChebyKAN) models complex nonlinear toxicity patterns. We evaluated MBFGNK using 5-fold cross-validation and an independent test set. The experimental results show that the ensemble achieved an AUC of 0.9687, an MCC of 0.8449, an Acc of 0.9221, and an F1 of 0.9205 on the independent test set, suggesting improved performance relative to previously reported baseline results on the same benchmark. Integrated gradients and modality-level analyses further identified prediction-informative motifs, residues, and spatial regions, providing interpretable evidence consistent with known characteristics of toxic peptides. These results suggest that MBFGNK is an effective and interpretable framework for peptide toxicity prediction and may assist in downstream safety-oriented peptide screening.

item.title: Synergy-Guided Molecular Redesign of Predicted P-Glycoprotein Substrates toward Synthetically Feasible Non-Substrates
item.description:
Abstract
Drug efflux mediated by P-glycoprotein (P-gp) remains a major barrier to effective small-molecule therapeutics, limiting both bioavailability and central nervous system exposure. While machine learning models can predict P-gp substrates, translating these predictions into actionable molecular design remains largely unexplored, particularly in enabling the rational conversion of substrates into nonsubstrates to mitigate efflux liability. Here, we introduce the synergy-guided fragment genetic algorithm (SF-GA), a computational framework that transforms predictive insight into an interpretable molecular design strategy. By integrating fragment synergy analysis into the mutation stage of a genetic algorithm, SF-GA biases fragment replacement toward co-occurring substructures associated with nonsubstrate classification, enabling interpretability at the chemical structure level and property-directed molecular optimization. Compared with genetic-algorithm and reinforcement-learning baselines under a fixed function-evaluation budget, SF-GA achieves competitive optimization performance while producing molecules with the highest retrosynthetic accessibility among all methods tested. Unlike the baselines, every accepted mutation is reported together with the discarded and inserted fragments and their synergy scores, providing a fragment-level rationale for each structural change; ablation against an unguided and an importance-only control isolates the contribution of bit co-occurrence. The method enables scaffold-preserving and similarity-constrained editing that converts P-gp substrates into predicted nonsubstrates. Docking against two human P-gp structures reveals weaker predicted binding for molecules with higher predicted nonsubstrate probability, motivating future experimental evaluation of P-gp transport.

item.title: An Integrated Computational-Experimental Workflow for Fungal Peroxygenase Discovery and Enzyme–Substrate Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Recent advances in enzyme informatics have produced increasingly powerful general models for the prediction of protein function prediction. However, their performance remains limited for underexplored enzyme families where experimental data are scarce and heterologous expression remains challenging. Here, we present a computational-experimental workflow for prioritizing, characterizing, and modeling fungal unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) as a case study in enzyme discovery under data-limited conditions. The workflow integrates large-scale sequence mining, expression-aware candidate prioritization, systematic experimental screening, and machine-learning-based prediction of enzyme–substrate activity. From more than 3000 mined candidate sequences, 59 putative UPOs were shortlisted, expressed in Escherichia coli across two batches, and tested against colorimetric substrates, yielding 27 UPOs with consistent expression and activity. A subset of 15 novel UPOs and 4 well-characterized reference enzyme sequences was then screened against a chemically diverse panel of 27 substrates to generate an enzyme–substrate activity data set. Using this data set, we developed two complementary machine learning protocols based on gradient boosting: (i) a structure-informed model incorporating homology modeling, docking, and interaction-derived features (modeling-docking-ML) and (ii) a latent-representation model utilizing joint protein/chemical language model embeddings (protein/chemical-language-model-ML). In retrospective validation, the models achieved performance with a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of up to 55% and accuracy up to 78%. In selected prospective testing on previously unseen batch 2 enzymes, the models achieved an MCC of up to 48% and accuracy up to 70%. Taken together, these results demonstrate that targeted experimental data generation, combined with complementary structure-informed and embedding-based models, can support prioritization and activity prediction within poorly characterized enzyme families while highlighting the continued challenge of generalizing to broader chemical substrate space.

item.title: Kinase Inhibitors can Change Protonation or Tautomeric State upon Binding
item.description:
Abstract
The binding affinity of a ligand to a protein is influenced by the protonation and tautomeric states of both partners. However, this relationship remains under-investigated due to the limited availability of computational tools capable of treating charge and tautomer states together in a scalable manner to study clinically relevant systems. Here, we use multi-conformation continuum electrostatics (MCCE) to calculate the protonation and tautomer distributions of nine kinase domains bound to 18 FDA-approved inhibitors across 37 cocrystal structures, while considering their Boltzmann-ensemble. The full pipeline was repeated in triplicate, so that every reported value carries a measured run-to-run uncertainty. Our simulations show that protein net charge and proton distribution remain largely stable even upon binding charged inhibitors. Our results find that individual inhibitor charges are dynamic, frequently increasing or decreasing upon binding a specific protein target. We observe that kinase-inhibitor binding shifts the relative probabilities of low-energy states (ΔG < 2.8 kcal/mol), but does not increase the probability of higher-energy states in the bound form. By considering all low-energy charge states and tautomers, we identify when two solution-state tautomers of nearly equal population resolve upon binding into a single state, creating free energy differences of up to 3.5 kcal/mol between tautomers, and in some complexes differences beyond the resolution of the sampling. In turn, we find that minority species can become the dominant component in the bound state, emphasizing the necessity of considering ensemble-wide protonation and tautomer states to accurately predict protein–ligand binding energetics.

item.title: Ga 3+ Replacing of Fe 3+ as a “Trojan Horse” Antimicrobial Strategy: Modeling the Process within Bacterial Catalase–Peroxidase KatG
item.description:
Abstract
Replacement of Fe3+ by Ga3+ has emerged as a promising “Trojan horse” antimicrobial strategy in response to the growing threat of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Because many bacterial proteins hijack host iron to sustain essential redox processes, substitution with redox inactive Ga3+, which closely resembles Fe3+ in ionic radius but possesses only one oxidation state, can disrupt their activity. Among potential targets, bacterial catalase-peroxidase shows particular sensitivity to Fe3+/Ga3+ exchange. However, the structural determinants and thermodynamic driving forces governing this substitution remain poorly understood. Here we combine ad hoc force field development, molecular dynamics simulations, alchemical free energy calculations, and QM/MM methods to elucidate the molecular basis of Fe3+/Ga3+ exchange in the bacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG. Our simulations show that the axial coordination environment of the heme B cofactor is largely preserved upon metal substitution, while the distal ligand dynamically alternates between histidine and a coordinated water molecule. Energy decomposition analysis reveals residue specific differences in electrostatic and van der Waals interactions following metal exchange. Free energy calculations indicate that substitution of iron by gallium in the KatG active site is thermodynamically favorable. The presence of a coordinated water molecule emerges as a key structural feature in both metalated states, while distinct binding patterns contribute differently to the overall thermodynamic driving force. These results provide an atomistic description of gallium mediated metal substitution in KatG and offer mechanistic insight into gallium-based antimicrobial strategies, supporting the rational design of new iron-mimetic antibacterial agents.

item.title: Interpretive Limits of Cross-Split AUPRC Differences in Deep Learning-Based Antibiotic Screening
item.description:
Abstract
Deep learning expands the chemical space accessible to antibiotic discovery, making interpretation of evaluation results increasingly important when only a few compounds can be prioritized from vast candidate libraries. AUPRC depends on test-set prevalence, while molecular splitting can alter training-to-test structural relatedness and test-set class composition, so when prevalence differs across splits, a cross-split AUPRC difference alone cannot quantify how much of the performance change is attributable to structural differences. Cross-split comparisons should therefore report test-set size, positive count, prevalence, splitting method, and the precision-recall summary metric, while direct model comparisons should use the same fixed independent test set whenever possible. Claims about practical screening utility should also consider top-k performance, early enrichment metrics, or prospective experimental hit rates under a prespecified budget, so that evidence remains aligned with the scientific claims it is intended to support.

item.title: Building a Physically Interpretable Compressed Chemical Space via Grid-Based Optimization
item.description:
Abstract
In recent years, deep generative models have been increasingly adopted for molecular optimization and design. In many such models, molecules are encoded into latent spaces that provide compact representations of their features. However, these latent spaces remain difficult to interpret in physical terms, and it is unclear how much structural and molecular information is retained under compression. This limitation becomes especially important when molecular behavior depends on specific three-dimensional arrangements embedded in an environmental context. Here, we introduce COMPRESS (Compression Of Molecular Physical fields into Reduced Spatial Sites), an optimization framework that represents a small molecule using a fixed number of physically parametrized spatial sites. Each site is defined by three spatial coordinates and three interaction parameters, yielding a fixed-size representation that remains directly interpretable in physical terms. To preserve molecular information, COMPRESS representations are optimized to reproduce the density, electrostatic, and van der Waals fields of the corresponding all-atom molecule on discretized three-dimensional grids. We systematically evaluate how molecular information is retained as the number of sites, K, is reduced. Our analysis covers benzene, 20 chemically diverse chemical scaffolds, benzene dimers, protein–ligand complexes, and 10,000 molecules chosen from the GEOM-Drugs data set. Across systems, field agreement deteriorates slowly at high resolution and then undergoes a rapid, pronounced transition at lower resolution. We further find that K = 25 conformers capture about 97% of the molecules from GEOM-Drugs under a loss threshold of 0.05, which we use as an indicator of fidelity. These results show that COMPRESS can provide a fixed-size, physically interpretable molecular representation, enabling compression to be evaluated directly using molecular interaction fields and resulting physical quantities. We also introduce a decoder that reconstructs all-atom structures directly from a COMPRESS representation, showing that the representation can support molecular generation in addition to field-preservation analysis. Finally, rationally modified COMPRESS representations through changes to site charge and size or the addition or removal of sites are shown to generate realistic chemical compounds upon decoding.

item.title: Cross-Modal Semantic Alignment for Cold-Start Drug–Target Interaction Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Drug–target interaction (DTI) prediction is essential for drug discovery, yet existing models often suffer from limited generalization when drugs or targets are unseen during training. This challenge is particularly severe in cold-start settings, where interaction records are unavailable for novel entities and effective semantic transfer between chemical and biological spaces is required. To address this problem, we propose CMA-DTI, a cross-modal semantic alignment framework for cold-start drug–target interaction prediction. CMA-DTI first extracts drug and protein representations from pretrained sequence models, and then it uses a dual-channel encoder to capture local functional patterns and global contextual dependencies. A bidirectional cross-modal alignment module is further introduced to model interactions between drug functional groups and protein binding regions, enabling fine-grained semantic transfer across heterogeneous modalities. Experiments on four benchmark data sets show that CMA-DTI achieves competitive performance in warm-start settings and improves generalization in challenging target cold-start and blind-start scenarios. Ablation studies and structural visualizations further support the contribution of the proposed modules and suggest residue-level interpretability for protein–ligand binding analysis.

item.title: CASyM: Chemotype Annotation through Synthesis Mapping
item.description:
Abstract
The identification and annotation of chemotypes is central to structure–activity relationship studies and property optimization in drug discovery. Current computational approaches rely on predefined fragmentation rules or structural similarity to identify these molecular scaffolds, often overlooking the rich information available in reaction data. Here, we introduce CASyM (Chemotype Annotation through Synthesis Mapping), a novel approach that leverages hierarchical reaction data to systematically identify chemotypes within compound libraries. CASyM constructs synthesis graphs from curated reaction data sets, detects major common intermediates, and builds chemotype graphs that capture the hierarchical and interconnected nature of chemical synthesis. SMARTS patterns are extracted to define chemotypes, enabling robust assignment of target molecules, including those absent from the original reaction data. We demonstrate the approach across three case studies using public patent data, proprietary electronic laboratory notebook data from drug discovery projects, and simulated multistep synthesis data for compounds lacking experimental synthesis records. CASyM achieves high coverage of target molecules (85–99%), reveals chemotype-property relationships, and enables chemotype assignment in the absence of experimental data. This reaction-centric approach provides a powerful framework for chemotype annotation, facilitating series exploration and optimization in medicinal chemistry.

item.title: Subpocket-Aware Fragment-Based Docking Pipeline for Kinase Ligand Design: Methodology and a PKA Case Study
item.description:
Abstract
Protein kinases regulate signal transduction through phosphorylation, and their dysregulation drives diseases like cancer, autoimmune disorders, and Alzheimer’s, making them key drug targets. Fragment-based drug design offers a powerful route to kinase inhibitors but often neglects kinase-specific structural insights. While KinFragLib, a library consisting of 7486 fragments derived from kinase-ligand complexes, provides a rich resource, exhaustive recombination of its fragments is computationally demanding. Here, we present an efficient exploration strategy that integrates subpocket-guided fragment growing with template docking to navigate this vast chemical space. Our automated pipeline prioritizes kinase-specific structural information, enabling targeted generation of chemically diverse ligands. Applied to the PKA kinase, the approach produced 33758 candidate molecules with promising docking scores, of which 15 were synthesized. Seven molecules reduced kinase activity by more than 50% at an inhibitor concentration of 100 μM, and five of these compounds also showed promising efficacy at a concentration of 10 μM. The IC50 determination ultimately revealed that five of the molecules were effective in the two- to three-digit nanomolar range. Crystallographic validation confirmed the predicted binding mode of the most potent compound. This methodology demonstrates how structure-informed guidance can transform fragment-based design into a scalable route for discovering novel kinase inhibitors.

item.title: UCEC: A Knowledge Graph-Assisted Machine Learning for Molecular-Mechanism-Interpretable Natural Product-Disease Association Prioritization
item.description:
Abstract
Natural products (NPs) have been considered a critical source of therapeutic drugs, but prioritizing NP-disease associations remain challenging because supporting evidence is distributed across multiple ingredients, targets, protein interactions, and pathways. Herein, we propose a knowledge graph-assisted machine learning model: Uncertainty-Calibrated Evidence-Chains (UCEC) for prioritizing NP-disease associations. UCEC separates predicted association strength from the evidence-conditioned stability of local mechanistic support. On a proxy benchmark designed to recover graph-supported indirect associations, evidence-chain integration increased Hits@50 from 0.392 to 0.509, with 68.8% of NPs indicating improved per-NP AUPRC. Source-separated validation using HERB 2.0 clinical trial records further supported candidate prioritization. Thus, UCEC provides a reliability-aware approach for prioritizing graph-supported NP-disease candidates and generating traceable mechanistic hypotheses for subsequent validation.

item.title: Integrating Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics, β-Variational Autoencoders, and Markov State Models Reveals the Activation Landscape of FGFR3 Kinase
item.description:
Abstract
Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) kinase plays a crucial role in cellular differentiation, proliferation, and skeletal development. Activation of the kinase domain through phosphorylation regulates the downstream signaling cascades, and its dysregulation leads to human dwarfism, skeletal dysplasia, and multiple cancers. However, the mechanistic basis of FGFR3 regulation by phosphorylation and ligand binding remains unclear. Here, we introduce an integrated GaMD-βVAE-MSM pipeline, a hybrid physics-ML framework for studying kinase activation. Gaussian-accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) enhances simulations by reducing the energy barrier. The variational autoencoder with tunable regularization was used for nonlinear dimension reduction and identifying slow collective variables. The Markov state model (MSM) was used for identifying metastable states spanning active-inactive conformations. Our results show that phosphorylation drives pronounced domain rearrangement and activation-loop dynamics. The coordinated movement of the molecular brake and regulatory spine governs the kinase activation. Ligand interaction stabilizes the active phosphorylated state with a free energy of −19 kcal/mol. Protein structure network analysis uncovers the long-range allosteric pathways. The potential regulatory sites involving αCβ4, β34, and β45 loops can be further exploited for allosteric intervention. Overall, this study highlights that phosphorylation and ligand binding dual regulate FGFR3 kinase through allosteric communication networks. The integrated GaMD−βVAE–MSM pipeline provides mechanistic insights into FGFR3 activation and may help the rational design of next-generation FGFR3-targeted therapeutics resistant to gatekeeper mutants.

item.title: scikit-fingerprints : A Python Library for Scikit-Learn-Compatible Molecular Fingerprints and Chemoinformatics
item.description:
Abstract
We present scikit-fingerprints, a comprehensive, fully scikit-learn-compatible library for molecular machine learning in Python, based on RDKit. Molecular fingerprints and related functionalities are workhorses of chemoinformatics, yet the widely used open-source frameworks are not compatible with the wider Python machine-learning ecosystem based on scikit-learn conventions. scikit-fingerprints closes this gap, bringing molecular fingerprints, molecular filters, similarity and distance measures, applicability domain estimation, data-splitting strategies, and more under a single familiar interface. Scikit-learn compatibility means that an entire chemoinformatics workflow, from a raw SMILES string to a deployable model, can be assembled from composable building blocks and can reuse the mature tooling of the surrounding ecosystem. The underlying RDKit code makes the library familiar and extensible for custom chemoinformatics use cases. We put a strong focus on unified interfaces, ease of use, computational efficiency, customization, and extensibility. scikit-fingerprints makes molecular machine learning faster to prototype, easier to reproduce, and simpler to deploy.

item.title: Bridging the Markush Gap in Optical Chemical Structure Recognition via a CLIP-Derived Visual Backbone and Synthetic Data Generation
item.description:
Abstract
The rapidly growing chemical literature contains invaluable information for pharmaceutical research and molecular biology, yet manual extraction on a large scale is increasingly impractical. Optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR), which converts molecular depictions into machine-readable representations, provides a key route toward automated chemical information extraction. However, existing OCSR methods remain limited in recognizing Markush structures, which are widely used in chemical documents, particularly pharmaceutical patents, because of their structural complexity and the scarcity of annotated data. Here, we introduce CLIP-OCSR, an encoder-decoder framework that integrates a domain-adaptively pretrained CLIP-RN50 vision encoder with a transformer decoder for chemical structure recognition, with a focus on Markush representations. To address data scarcity, we developed a synthetic data generation strategy that produces diverse Markush images paired with pseudo-SMILES representations encoding substituent, frequency, and position variations. Benchmarking demonstrates that CLIP-OCSR achieves competitive performance on standard OCSR benchmarks and shows strong capability in recognizing Markush structures involving substituents and frequency variations. For structures with position variations, CLIP-OCSR generates pseudo-SMILES predictions that retain the corresponding positional information, enabling the downstream enumeration of possible positional isomers. Beyond image-only OCSR, we extend CLIP-OCSR toward multimodal Markush structure extraction by integrating graphical recognition with LLM-based textual variable-definition extraction, enabling downstream structure instantiation. Overall, this work advances automated recognition of complex chemical structures and provides a framework for the structured extraction of Markush information from chemical documents.

item.title: PDI-Spot: A Robust Representation Learning Framework for Identifying Energetic Hotspots in Protein–DNA Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
The binding affinity of protein–DNA complexes is concentrated within a subset of interface residues, called “hotspots”, which are critical for maintaining stable interactions. Therefore, identifying these energetic anchors is essential for elaborating on how mutations disrupt transcriptional regulation and for identifying druggable regions within disease-associated interfaces. In this study, we introduce our novel prediction model, PDI-Spot, that leverages representation learning to capture the complex features of protein–DNA interfaces. Unlike traditional methods that rely on limited, handcrafted descriptors, PDI-Spot extracts high-dimensional, structure- and sequence-driven representations to achieve better predictive performance. We trained the PDI-Spot model on a curated protein–DNA complex data set and rigorously validated its performance on an independent test set to ensure generalizability across different structural families. Following the extraction of residue-level embeddings, an optimal feature set was identified through a combined approach of minimum redundancy maximum relevance and multilayer perceptron architectures. By training a neural network on the optimal feature set, we developed a robust predictive framework for hotspot identification. On an independent test set, PDI-Spot achieved an AUROC of 0.809, an F1-score of 0.667, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.625. We also verified via permutation tests that PDI-Spot captures biologically meaningful patterns beyond random chance. PDI-Spot consistently demonstrates competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, providing a reliable model for mapping the energetic landscapes of protein–DNA interfaces. The source code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/ebsrn0/pdi-spot.git.

item.title: Evaluation of Physics-Based Pose Prediction and the Role of Receptor Flexibility in a Community Antiviral Blind Challenge
item.description:
Abstract
Prediction of protein–ligand binding modes is a key step in computer-aided drug design, since incorrect pose prediction inevitably limits the achievable accuracy of downstream physics-based affinity predictions. The ASAP-Polaris-OpenADMET antiviral competition was launched in 2025 as a means to prospectively test computational methods across a range of measurements that guide early prioritization during a drug discovery campaign including pose prediction. Here, we describe our two open-source, physics-based entries to the pose prediction challenge, which are based on templated molecular growth with hybrid machine learning/molecular mechanics interatomic potentials. We show that our approach was among the top-performing physics-based methods, and with a retrospective change to the workflow to make greater use of the training data as templates, we obtain a success rate of 74% across SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV main protease target protein structures. Finally, we investigate the importance of receptor side-chain flexibility on retrospective performance. We find that building poses against an ensemble of feasible side-chain conformers is useful in generating improved binding poses but that the tested scoring functions are unable to successfully pick out native structures from the generated ensemble.

item.title: TMC-LewisGen: Automated Generation of Lewis-like Structures for Transition–Metal Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Lewis structures constitute a foundational language in chemical education, mechanistic reasoning, synthesis, and modern cheminformatics. With the accelerating shift toward data-driven and AI-assisted molecular science, the ability to rapidly generate Lewis-like representations, including RDKit-parsable SMILES, has become essential for large-scale analysis and predictive modeling. While mature tools exist for organic molecules, transition-metal complexes (TMCs) remain systematically underserved owing to their inherently diverse coordination patterns. To address this gap, we develop TMC-LewisGen, an automated tool for generating Lewis-like structures of TMCs directly from Cartesian coordinates. The task is formulated as a discrete variable optimization problem, where a comprehensive set of explicit chemical rules defines the feasible solution space and integer linear programming (ILP) identifies a globally optimal assignment of bond orders, lone pairs, and formal charges, followed by postprocessing corrections. The final outputs include Lewis-like structures, RDKit-parsable SMILES, and interpretive bonding reports framed within the covalent bond classification (CBC) formalism, in which ligands are categorized as L-, X-, or Z- type donors. Benchmarking on nearly 29,000 TMCs demonstrates robust performance, with valid SMILES generated for 100% of the structures and subsecond ILP solution times in most cases. Representative examples, including Werner-type complexes, η-coordinated π-ligands, and metal–carbene motifs, demonstrate broad applicability. The framework supports large-scale structural annotation, automated chemical interpretation, and data-driven modeling of TMCs. A freely accessible web server for 3D TMC analysis and visualization is available at https://tmc-lewis-structure.streamlit.app/.

item.title: e MolFrag 2 and e Synth 2: Sound Fragment-Based Molecular Decomposition and Reconstruction
item.description:
Abstract
We present eMolFrag2 and eSynth2, enhanced successors to eMolFrag and eSynth for fragment-based molecular decomposition and reconstruction. eMolFrag2 is a complete reimplementation of eMolFrag in Python, using RDKit and graph-based molecular representations to preserve connectivity, identify free atoms, combine adjacent linkers, and avoid aromaticity ambiguities that impair downstream reconstruction. eSynth2 generalizes fragment recombination by removing hard-coded molecular-property filters, supporting multiple bonds to a single brick atom, and adding a targeted reconstruction mode for soundness validation. Across 36,534 nonredundant DUD-E active compounds, the eMolFrag2 → eSynth2 workflow reconstructed every input molecule exactly (Tanimoto coefficient, TC = 1.0), whereas the original eMolFrag→ eSynth workflow reconstructed 51 of the 100 molecules in a benchmark subset. The upgraded workflow also produced broader recombinant chemical spaces, including higher entropy in a four-molecule diversity analysis (2.78 versus 2.70). Both tools are open-source, platform-agnostic, and available for academic and commercial use.

item.title: Latent Style-Based Quantum Wasserstein GAN for Drug Design
item.description:
Abstract
The development of new drugs is a tedious, time-consuming, and expensive process for which the average costs are estimated to be up to around $2.5 billion. The first step in this long process is the design of the new drug, for which de novo drug design, assisted by artificial intelligence, has blossomed in recent years and has revolutionized the field.
